title: Why Students Should Annotate Their ChatGPT Chats
author: Doan Winkel
summary: Winkel argues that teachers who collect student ChatGPT logs only to hunt for cheating are wasting the richest new assessment artifact available. He reframes the chat transcript as a text to be annotated, like a short story or lab notebook, so that students explain their own intent, strategy and evaluation of the AI. The move borrows the logic of the math teacher who grades steps rather than answers, and applies it to the AI era. He shows how a transcript plus annotations diagnoses root causes quickly, using a student who asked whether Romeo and Juliet is boring because he never understood the assignment. The post then supplies a practical kit: a four-question annotation key, a three-question debrief, a lightweight rubric, subject variations and fixes for common failure modes. His closing advice is to use annotation sparingly, a couple of times a semester, as a deep-dive assessment of AI use rather than a weekly routine.
points: Treating AI chats as evidence of process rather than evidence of dishonesty turns a surveillance chore into a formative assessment.
Annotation hands the interpretive work to students, building metacognition and AI literacy at once.
Transcripts expose the real problem: the Romeo and Juliet example was a failure to read the assignment, not AI abuse, so the fix is teaching assignment reading, not writing a policy.
Low stakes matter: grading students on whether they can explain their use, not whether the use was good, keeps them from hiding it.
Because annotated chats are heavy to design and read, Winkel recommends them only a couple of times per course per semester, sampling or skimming to avoid drowning.
quotes: If you’re asking students to paste their ChatGPT logs into a doc, then you skim them quickly to see whether they cheated, you’re wasting the most valuable new assessment artifact you’ve had in years.
Math teachers solved the calculator problem a long time ago. They didn’t ban calculators forever. They said: “You can use the tool. But I still need to see your reasoning.

Instead of you doing all the interpretation, you push the metacognition back on students. You ask them to annotate their own chat and explain what they were trying to do, what worked, and what they would do differently next time.

Looking at the chat and the context, it became clear the root issue was that the student had skimmed the project menu and never actually understood the task. The misunderstanding was about reading, not “AI abuse.

Students who are already confident with tech will use AI no matter what you do. Students who are less confident or more afraid of being accused of cheating will hold back unless they know how to use it and how to talk about their use.

Tell them you aren’t grading them on whether their AI use was “good” or “bad,” you’re grading them on whether they can explain what they were doing. This is crucial. If the first experience with annotation feels like a trap, they will go right back to hiding their AI use.
Annotated chats are powerful, but they’re heavy; they take time to design and time to read. Don’t do this every week. In my experience, a couple times a semester per course is plenty.
